content: This report reviews the 2025 operating performance of the Northfield assembly plant. Overall production efficiency, measured as overall equipment effectiveness (OEE), peaked at 92% in Q2 and ended the year at 81% in Q4. Total output for the year was 506,000 units. Management remains committed to the annual target of 85% average efficiency. The plant operates three production lines across two shifts. Line 3, which produces the high-volume gearbox housing, accounts for roughly 45% of total output and therefore dominates the plant-level results. Safety performance was stable with no lost-time incidents recorded in the year.

Northfield employs 240 people, of whom 168 work directly on the production lines. Investment in 2025 focused on automation of the packaging area and on a new quality inspection station at the end of Line 2. The product mix was unchanged from 2024, so differences between quarters are attributable to operating conditions rather than mix.

Table 1 gives the quarterly efficiency, output and scrap rate. Efficiency is the product of availability, performance and quality as defined in the plant KPI handbook. Table 1: Quarterly production efficiency, output and scrap rate, 2025. Figure 1: Production efficiency by quarter (%), bar chart with trend line. The chart shows efficiency rising from 78% in Q1 to a peak of 92% in Q2, followed by a steady decline through Q3 (85%) and Q4 (81%).

section: 4. Analysis of the Q2 to Q4 Decline
content: Efficiency fell by 11 percentage points between Q2 (92%) and Q4 (81%), a relative decline of about 12.0%. Three main reasons explain the change: Reason 1 - Rising mechanical failures on Line 3. Ageing spindle bearings caused repeated unplanned stops. Mechanical failure downtime grew from 28 hours in Q2 to 71 hours in Q4 (see the Maintenance Summary 2025). Reason 2 - Raw material shortages. A supplier delay for cast aluminium blanks starved the lines in the second half. Material shortage downtime rose from 9 hours in Q2 to 38 hours in Q4. Reason 3 - Staffing turnover and training. Eleven experienced operators left in Q3 and were replaced by trainees, which lowered line speed and raised the scrap rate from 2.2% in Q2 to 3.0% in Q4.

For 2026 the plant will replace the Line 3 spindle bearings in the Q1 planned shutdown, dual-source the aluminium blanks, and introduce a structured four-week onboarding program. These measures target a return to at least 88% efficiency by Q2 2026.
Northfield assembly plant - Maintenance Department annual review

This summary records equipment downtime at Northfield for 2025, grouped by cause and quarter. It complements the Factory Operations Report 2025, which discusses the effect of downtime on production efficiency. Downtime hours are counted across all three production lines. Planned maintenance is a fixed 40 hours per quarter and is included in the totals.
Table 2: Downtime hours by cause and quarter, 2025. Total downtime was lowest in Q2 at 119 hours and highest in Q4 at 204 hours, an increase of 85 hours.

Mechanical failure is the largest single cause of unplanned downtime, increasing from 28 hours in Q2 to 71 hours in Q4. Root-cause analysis traced most events to worn spindle bearings on Line 3. Figure 2: Downtime hours by cause per quarter, stacked bars.

Bearing inspections were moved from quarterly to monthly in Q3. A spare spindle assembly was purchased in Q4 to shorten repair time. Electrical faults stayed roughly flat at 14 to 22 hours per quarter.

Replace all Line 3 spindle bearings during the planned Q1 2026 shutdown, hold a minimum safety stock of cast aluminium blanks, and review the planned maintenance allowance of 40 hours per quarter once bearing replacement is complete.

Cumulative Distribution Evaluation of Machine Learning Features Using Random Variables 
I. Practical Significance. Cumulative Distribution Analysis plays a fundamental role in understanding machine learning features by 
interpreting them as random variables governed by probability distributions. By computing the CDF 
𝑃(𝑋≤𝑥), this practicum enables learners to analyze  the probability structure, spread, skewness, and 
concentration of feature values within a dataset.

Unlike simple descriptive statistics such as mean and 
variance, the CDF provides a complete probabilistic view of how data accumulates across its range, which 
is essential for threshold -based decision -making, anomaly detection, and feature scaling. In predictive 
modelling, CDF analysis helps identify outliers, assess distribution stability, and compare feature behavior 
across different classes or populations. Furthermore, it strengthens conceptual understanding of random 
variables, empirical probability, and statistical inference —core mathematical foundations underlying 
machine learning algorithms.

Thus, this practicum bridges probability theory with real-world data analytics, 
enhancing interpretability and reliability in model development. II Competency and Industry-Specific Practical Skills

Minimum Underpinning Theory (Include relevant content & images for this practicum.) 
Computing the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of a machine learning dataset is fundamentally 
grounded in the theory of random variables and probability distributions.

If a feature is modeled as a random variable X, its cumulative distribution function is defined as  
𝐹(𝑥)=𝑃(𝑋≤𝑥), which represents the probability that the variable takes a value less than or equal to a 
specified threshold. For continuous variables, the CDF is obtained by integrating the probability density function (PDF), , while 
for discrete variables it is computed as a summation of probability mass values. In practical machine learning datasets, the empirical CDF is estimated from observed data by ordering the 
sample values and assigning cumulative relative frequencies, thereby approximating the theoretical 
distribution.

The CDF acts as a normalization mechanism, ensuring probabilities remain bounded between 
0 and 1 and providing a complete probabilistic description of the feature.

Unlike mean or variance, which 
summarize central tendency or spread, the CDF captures the entire accumulation behavior of data across its 
domain.

Theoretically, it supports threshold-based classification, quantile computation, anomaly detection, 
and distribution comparison between classes.

By interpreting features as realizations of random variables,

XV. Interpretation of Results (Students to state the meaning of the above-obtained results/observations)

The results demonstrate the evaluation of the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) across 
three machine learning scenarios modeled via discrete random variables: CPU-intensive requests, lost 
network packets, and suspicious login attempts. For CPU-intensive requests, the cumulative 
probability F(3) = 0.90 indicates a 90% probability that 3 or fewer requests arrive. For packet losses 
and suspicious login attempts, F(2) = 0.70 and F(3) = 0.90 show that 70% and 90% of observed 
occurrences fall at or below 2 and 3 events, respectively. CDF analysis effectively captures data 
accumulation for setting system thresholds, capacity management, and security alerting.

XVI. Conclusions (Students to draw conclusions (or take decisions) based on the interpretation of results)

Thus, the Python programs were successfully executed using NumPy to calculate and visualize the 
Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) across CPU request loads, packet loss events, and 
suspicious login security features. The cumulative probabilities verified how probability accumulates 
across feature thresholds, establishing a quantitative foundation for risk profiling, anomaly detection, 
and decision-making in machine learning environments.

A C T I V I T Y 2
Quick Check — Predict the Output
QUIZ
What does this print?
if ("String".replace('t','T') ==
 "String".replace('t','T'))
 System.out.println("Equal");
else
 System.out.println("Not Equal");
Answer & Why
Output: "Not Equal"
Each call to replace() returns a new String object in 
memory. == checks whether two references point to the 
same object — not whether their contents match — so 
two separately-created "String" results are never == equal, 
even though .equals() would say true.

content:
D Y N A M I C S T R I N G G E N E R A T I O N
String Templates — Java's Journey STR
1 A "string template" means combining fixed text with variable values computed at runtime — the core idea behind dynamic text-
processing output (emails, reports, JSON, SQL). 2 Java proposed a native interpolation syntax — String Templates — using STR."Hello \{name}" as JEP 430 (preview, JDK 21) and JEP 459 
(second preview, JDK 22). 3 A third preview, JEP 465, was planned for JDK 23 — but after community feedback, Oracle concluded the design was unsuitable and 
withdrew it in March 2024. JDK 23 shipped with no string templates at all.

section: D Y N A M I C S T R I N G G E N E R A T I O N
content:
4 As of today, Java has no built-in string-interpolation syntax like Python's f-strings or JavaScript's template literals — the feature may 
return in a redesigned form, but there is no confirmed timeline.

5 In practice, Java developers achieve the same goal — dynamic string templates — using String.format(), printf(), text blocks with 
.formatted(), and MessageFormat, covered on the next slides.

JEP 430 (JDK 21) → JEP 459 (JDK 22) → JEP 465 WITHDRAWN (JDK 23, March 2024)

Text Blocks & formatted() """
DEFINITION
A text block (Java 13+, delimited by triple quotes """) holds 
multi-line literal text. 
Calling .formatted(args) on it works exactly like 
String.format(), making text blocks ideal for multi-line 
templates such as emails, HTML, JSON, or SQL.

 """;
String result = 
templateText.formatted(args...)
CODE SNIPPET

 Dear %s,
 Your order %s has shipped.
 """;

Your order ORD1042 has shipped.

section: S T R I N G F U N C T I O N
content:
S T R I N G F U N C T I O N
MessageFormat — Locale-Aware Templates {0}
DEFINITION
MessageFormat builds strings from a pattern using 
numbered placeholders {0}, {1}, ... instead of type-based 
specifiers. 
It is especially useful for internationalized (i18n) messages 
that must adapt to different locales.
SYNTAX
static String format(String pattern, 
Object... args)
Placeholders refer to argument position, not type — the same argument 
can even be reused at multiple positions in the pattern.
CODE SNIPPET
String name = "Meera";
int age = 21;
String msg = MessageFormat.format(
 "Hello {0}, you are {1} years old.", name, age);
System.out.println(msg);
OUTPUT
Hello Meera, you are 21 years old.

Choosing the Right Templating Technique ?
Situation Best Choice
One-off simple message + concatenation
Building text inside a loop StringBuilder
Fixed pattern with placeholders String.format()
Printing directly to console printf()
Multi-line templates (email, HTML, SQL, JSON) Text block + .formatted()
Locale / language-sensitive output MessageFormat
Key takeaway: Java has no built-in interpolation syntax — String.format()/.formatted() is the standard way to generate dynamic string 
templates today.

1.0 Rationale (Students should elaborate on the importance/significance of doing this project, in about 200 to

section: OBCFC - Micro-Project Proposal (2025-26) Division of Computer Science and Engineering
content:
The micro -project titled "Fluid Flow in a Jet Nozzle using Vector Calculus" focuses on understanding the 
fundamental behavior of fluid flow in jet nozzles, which are widely used in aerospace, aerodynamics, 
propulsion systems, and fluid machinery industries to generate thrust.Jet nozzles are essential devices used to 
accelerate fluid pressure to high velocities and convert pressure energy into kinetic energy, enabling thrust 
generation in aircraft engines and rockets.

section: OBCFC - Micro-Project Proposal (2025-26) Division of Computer Science and Engineering
content:
This project is significant because it bridges theoretical mathematical concepts with real -world engineering 
applications.Vector calculus provides powerful tools such as velocity vectors (speed and direction control), 
gradient (pressure variance), divergen ce (spread or shrink flow), and continuity equations (conservation of 
mass), which are essential to describe and analyze fluid motion.By simulating these parameters, students 
develop analytical thinking and gain early exposure to simulation techniques simi lar to Computational Fluid 
Dynamics (CFD), commonly used in the industry for design and optimization.

section: OBCFC - Micro-Project Proposal (2025-26) Division of Computer Science and Engineering
content:
Academically, the project supports the attainment of course outcomes CO2 (data structures), CO3 (Object -
Oriented Programming), and CO5 (image processing/visualization).Overall, this project builds a strong 
foundation in fluid dynamics and aerospace enginee ring concepts while applying modern computational tools 
like Python.

2.0 Literature Review (Students should provide the relevant knowledge/information and existing status, from 
journals/technical magazines, brochures, websites and other sources referred/required to complete the 
selected micro-project in about 200 to 500 words.)

section: OBCFC - Micro-Project Proposal (2025-26) Division of Computer Science and Engineering
content:
Jet nozzle fluid dynamics has been extensively studied using computational methods, focusing on vector -
based flow analysis for thrust optimization.Recent research by Atmaca (2021) utilized CFD simulations to 
analyze exit velocities in rectangular nozzles, revealing how geometry impacts flow characteristics like 
maximum velocity—insights directly applicable to vector field modelling.

section: OBCFC - Micro-Project Proposal (2025-26) Division of Computer Science and Engineering
content:
In terms of Python -based simulations, Stam’s "Stable Fluids" (2003) remains a foundational work, allowing 
for real-time 2D CFD using Navier -Stokes solvers.These implementations often align with Course Outcome 
CO2 by using lists for grids and dictionaries for fields, and CO5 by using OpenCV for quiver plots to visualize 
velocity vectors.Further advancements by researchers like Ravi Ram demonstrate the use of Python for 
generating structured meshes and simulating rocket nozzles (e.g., PSLV), emphasizing the u se of Object -
Oriented Programming (OOP) for nozzle geometries.

section: OBCFC - Micro-Project Proposal (2025-26) Division of Computer Science and Engineering
content:
Current industry trends, such as METU’s CFD optimization (2024), highlight the necessity of vector calculus—
specifically divergence-free fields—in modeling subsonic jets.These studies inform our proposed simulation, 
where an OOP Nozzle class will process v ector data structures and visualize results through image 
enhancement techniques.This project aims to fill the gap in accessible Python prototypes for students, 
providing real-time visuals for educational thrust prediction.

3.0 Proposed Methodology (Students should provide a detailed Flowchart/Procedure in brief (about 200 to 
500) that will be followed to complete the micro-project.)

section: OBCFC - Micro-Project Proposal (2025-26) Division of Computer Science and Engineering
content:
The methodology for this project is structured to systematically model fluid behavior through a jet nozzle by 
integrating theoretical fluid mechanics with computational analysis. Procedure: 
1. Geometric Configuration: Define the jet nozzle design (convergent or convergent-divergent) and establish 
assumptions such as steady, incompressible flow to simplify mathematical modeling. 2. Mathematical Formulation: Formulate the governing equations—Continuity, Momentum (Navier-Stokes), 
and Energy —using vector calculus.

section: OBCFC - Micro-Project Proposal (2025-26) Division of Computer Science and Engineering
content:
This includes using the Area of a Circle ($A = \pi r^2$) for cross -
sections and applying Bernoulli’s Theorem and the Equation of Continuity ($A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$) to 
determine pressure and velocity shifts.

3.

Vector Calculus Application: Apply vector operators such as gradient (for pressure distribution), 
divergence (for mass conservation), and curl to describe the velocity fields within the nozzle.
